strengths: Addresses genuine gap in VLM evaluation: First benchmark combining multimodal observations with strategic reasoning in multi-agent environments
Comprehensive experimental design: 8 diverse games, 14 models across reasoning/chat/open-source categories, two complementary evaluation dimensions (offline reasoning + online decision-making)
Rigorous dataset construction with documented principles (predictable, diverse, balanced) and detailed generation protocols for each environment
Valuable analytical insights including surprising finding that multimodal observations sometimes hurt performance, systematic failure case analysis, and social behavior visualization
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, comprehensive appendix, promise of code/data release, clear experimental protocols
Well-presented results with actionable insights on test-time scaling, multimodal effectiveness, and strategic decision-making limitations across game types
weaknesses: Limited environmental scope: Primarily 2-player games, relatively simple environments (grid-worlds, board games). Claim about 'multi-agent environments' not fully supported given focus on 2-player scenarios

Critical findings underexplored: The striking result that text-only observations outperform multimodal ones lacks investigation. Why does this occur? Only 3 games tested. This deserves dedicated study, not one subsection
Confounded evaluation: In video games, failures could stem from either perception or reasoning. No ablations to isolate these factors, making it unclear what capabilities are actually being measured

Methodological concerns: (1) Dataset generation uses heuristic strategies that may bias action distributions; (2) Self-play assumes symmetry but first/second-player roles differ; (3) Conventional agents don't adapt, limiting true strategic assessment; (4) Temperature=1.0 for all models without justification; (5) No significance testing despite high variance

Limited analysis depth: Failure cases are anecdotal rather than systematic; test-time scaling (CoT) only tested on 3 games; social behavior analysis is descriptive not explanatory; no cross-game pattern analysis
No proposed solutions: Paper is purely evaluative with no methods or architectural insights to address identified problems. Limited theoretical framework explaining performance gaps
Presentation issues: Figure 1 duplicated; key details relegated to 17-page appendix; missing preprocessing specifications for image sequences and text→action mappings

Generalization concerns: All 14 models are recent (2024-2025); unclear how findings generalize. Some environments too simple (Tic-Tac-Toe solved). Accuracy already far from random (47.8% vs 24.3%) suggesting potential ceiling effects

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Systematic evaluation of VLMs in multi-agent environments fills a real need, as existing benchmarks focus on single-agent settings
Comprehensive experimental scope: 14 leading VLMs, 8 diverse games, dual evaluation dimensions (offline strategic reasoning + online decision-making) represents substantial effort
Good coverage of game types: Cooperative (Hanabi, Overcooked), competitive (Breakthrough, Kuhn Poker, Pong), and mixed-motive (three social dilemmas) games provide diversity
Useful negative findings: Demonstrates that 6/14 models perform worse than random on decision-making, providing clear evidence of VLM limitations
Extensive supplementary material: Detailed environment specifications, evaluation protocols, and additional experiments increase transparency
weaknesses: Limited novelty in benchmark design: Most games are existing (Hanabi, Overcooked, Breakthrough, Kuhn Poker, Atari Pong); only Battle of the Colors is novel and relatively simple. Adaptation to visual format is straightforward, not innovative

Problematic dataset construction for strategic reasoning: (1) 90% of Hanabi data from VLM self-play (circular evaluation), (2) Breakthrough uses minimax with depth-limited search (not representative of natural play), (3) 400 samples is small without justification, (4) selection criteria ('diverse', 'balanced') are vaguely defined

Critical finding underdeveloped: Multimodal observations hurt performance compared to text-only (Finding 3), but only 3/8 games tested, text descriptions not detailed, and no investigation of why visual input degrades reasoning. This alarming result deserves central focus, not side analysis

Weak statistical rigor: (1) Only 10 decision-making episodes with high variance (σ ≈ μ or larger), (2) No significance testing or correction for multiple comparisons, (3) Large standard deviations make conclusions unreliable, (4) Normalized returns can be misleading with high variance

Insufficient validation of core claims: (1) 'Strategic reasoning' is a misnomer for next-action prediction; true reasoning involves multi-step lookahead and counterfactual thinking, (2) No human baseline (acknowledged limitation), making it impossible to assess if 47.8% accuracy is good or bad
Failure case analysis is qualitative: Only anecdotal examples in Section 4.4/Appendix F; no systematic categorization, quantification of prevalence, or analysis of whether cases are representative
Test-time scaling analysis lacks novelty: CoT helping performance is well-known; only tested on 3/8 games; comparison between reasoning models (which already reason) and chat+CoT models is unfair
Missing ablations and sensitivity analysis: No investigation of prompt formulation sensitivity, action representation (text vs. symbolic), information ordering, or visual encoding choices
Limited insights into why VLMs fail: Paper describes what VLMs struggle with but provides minimal guidance on why or how to improve. No mechanistic analysis of failure modes
Incomplete model coverage: o3 (cost) and gemini-2.5-pro (rate limits) not evaluated; o3 particularly relevant given reasoning focus
Game complexity limitations: Mostly 2-player games with small state spaces; real-world scenarios often involve >2 agents and imperfect communication

Questionable decision-making evaluation: Self-play with same model doesn't test real coordination; fixed opponent in competitive games doesn't capture adaptation; Atari Pong required adding step reward because score was too sparse, changing what's measured

strengths: Addresses an important gap in VLM evaluation by introducing the first multimodal benchmark for multi-agent strategic reasoning and decision-making
Comprehensive benchmark design with 8 carefully curated environments spanning cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive interactions grounded in game theory and MARL
Extensive evaluation of 14 state-of-the-art VLMs with rigorous experimental setup, proper baselines, and normalization schemes
Clear empirical findings including counterintuitive discoveries (e.g., multimodal observations can hurt performance vs. text-only) and insights on test-time scaling benefits
Excellent presentation with thorough appendices, detailed dataset construction procedures, and reproducibility documentation
Valuable qualitative failure case analysis providing concrete examples of VLM reasoning limitations
Two complementary evaluation dimensions (offline strategic reasoning and online decision-making) provide comprehensive assessment
weaknesses: Limited multi-agent scope: predominantly 2-player games despite 'multi-agent' framing; only Hanabi supports >2 players, undermining applicability to real-world multi-agent scenarios

Dataset construction relies on AI-generated trajectories (minimax, prediction models) rather than human demonstrations, introducing potential biases and limiting assessment of genuine strategic reasoning vs. algorithm mimicry

Shallow analysis of key findings: multimodal vs. text-only comparison limited to 3 environments; insufficient investigation of why adding visual information hurts performance; lacks systematic failure categorization
Missing human baseline for strategic reasoning despite being identified as a critical limitation; no evaluation against diverse opponent populations in competitive games

Limited metrics: strategic reasoning uses only accuracy (missing precision/recall/F1); normalized episode return may obscure fine-grained performance differences; no statistical significance testing between model groups
Incomplete reproducibility: code/data availability is a placeholder; specific prompts not provided; no computational cost analysis; missing details on prompt engineering and ablations

Minimal solution-oriented guidance: paper identifies problems effectively but offers limited recommendations for addressing them; no ablation studies on design choices like temperature or token limits
Potential confounds in evaluation: text-only descriptions quality unclear; dataset balance across strategies for mixed-motive games not discussed; distribution of different game states under-analyzed

strengths: Addresses important gap: First comprehensive multimodal benchmark for evaluating VLMs in multi-agent environments, filling a clear void where existing benchmarks focus on single-agent settings

Comprehensive evaluation framework: Three complementary evaluation dimensions (perception, strategic reasoning, decision-making) with careful dataset construction (400 samples per environment per type)
Extensive empirical coverage: Evaluation of 15 leading VLMs across multiple model families with detailed configurations; provides valuable empirical insights on current VLM capabilities
Thorough analysis and insights: Includes multimodal vs. text-only comparison, test-time scaling effects, social behavior analysis, human baselines (62.7% vs 31.4%), and detailed failure case analysis
Diverse game environments: Ten well-chosen games covering cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive interactions with different strategic requirements
Strong reproducibility commitment: Comprehensive appendices with implementation details and promise to release code/datasets
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with excellent visualizations and logical organization
weaknesses: Limited benchmark novelty: The 10 games are primarily visual adaptations of existing well-known games from MARL/game theory literature (Hanabi, Overcooked, Breakthrough) rather than fundamentally new evaluation challenges

Counterintuitive multimodal finding insufficiently explored: Section 4.1 shows VLMs perform better with text-only observations, undermining core premise but receiving only cursory investigation. Suggests either fundamental multimodal reasoning limitations or poor prompt design

Evaluation methodology concerns: (1) Strategic reasoning uses only next-action prediction as proxy, not equilibria understanding; (2) Decision-making evaluated over only 10 episodes—high variance, no statistical significance tests; (3) Limited opponent diversity (self-play or simple rule-based agents only); (4) Suboptimal oracle definitions (e.g., minimax depth 5 not guaranteed optimal)

Dataset construction biases: Datasets generated from strong models (o3) or hand-crafted heuristics may not reflect diverse strategic behaviors; action ratio balancing (e.g., 2:3:4 Hanabi) appears arbitrary
Limited multi-agent scope: Predominantly 2-player games; n-player extension (3-player) relegated to appendix with minimal analysis despite real-world relevance

Insufficient statistical rigor: No significance testing between models, limited error bars, human study with only 26 college students, no ablation on prompt design (temperature fixed at 1.0 for all models)

Incomplete analysis: No systematic correlation between game properties (Table 1 taxonomy) and performance; missing breakdown of deficient capabilities (spatial reasoning vs. theory-of-mind vs. planning); failure analysis mostly anecdotal
Simple environments and limited generalization: All relatively simple grid-worlds; unclear how insights transfer to complex, realistic multi-agent scenarios
Primarily empirical contribution: Paper documents problems but proposes no solutions; lacks technical innovation or methodological contributions beyond benchmark creation
Modest insights: Findings are somewhat expected (reasoning models outperform chat models; VLMs struggle with multi-agent reasoning); limited actionable guidance for improving VLMs

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 15 VLMs and 10 environments with proper statistical reporting
Addresses important gap of evaluating VLMs in multi-agent settings with visual observations
Includes human baseline (26 participants) providing meaningful context for performance comparison
Extensive supplementary analysis covering multimodal effects, test-time scaling, social behaviors, and failure cases
Well-organized benchmark design with clear taxonomy of environments (cooperative, competitive, mixed-motive) and required abilities
weaknesses: Critical methodological flaw: Strategic reasoning ground truth uses model predictions (Hanabi) and heuristic strategies (social dilemmas) rather than optimal/expert play, creating circular dependencies and overstating ToM capabilities

Major unexplained finding: Text-only observations outperform multimodal observations (e.g., 58.2% vs 61.2% for Hanabi), contradicting the paper's core premise—insufficient investigation of this counterintuitive result
Weak decision-making baselines: MCTS with only 100 simulations, minimax depth 5, single fixed opponents; limits conclusions about true strategic ability
Limited novelty: Environments are well-established; adaptation to vision-grounded setting is primarily an engineering contribution without algorithmic or methodological innovations
Shallow analysis with limited actionable insights: Identifies performance gaps but doesn't systematically explain causes or provide guidance for improvement; failure analysis is mostly anecdotal
Missing key investigations: Why do open-source models outperform reasoning models in mixed-motive games? Why does text outperform multimodal? No ablation studies on design choices

Evaluation design concerns: Two-player focus limits multi-agent complexity; human baseline with only 26 participants; comparison of VLMs to humans may not be entirely fair due to different training and embodied experience

strengths: Addresses an important gap: comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-agent VLM evaluation where prior work focuses only on single-agent scenarios
Comprehensive benchmark design: 10 well-curated vision-grounded environments covering cooperative, competitive, and mixed-motive games grounded in game theory and MARL
Rigorous experimental methodology: Three complementary evaluation dimensions (perception, strategic reasoning, decision-making) with 400 carefully constructed samples per environment
Thorough analysis and insights: Human experiments, multimodal observation ablations, test-time scaling effects, social behavior analysis, and detailed failure cases provide deep understanding
Excellent reproducibility: Extensive implementation details in appendices, promised code/data release, clear model configurations, and straightforward evaluation protocol
Broad model coverage: 15 state-of-the-art VLMs evaluated (reasoning, chat, open-source) providing comprehensive landscape assessment
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective visualizations and logical organization
weaknesses: Critical issue with multimodal design: Text-only observations consistently outperform multimodal observations (Section 4.1, Tables 7-8), contradicting the benchmark's core premise that visual information is essential. This deserves thorough investigation and redesign before publication

Limited scope of multi-agent complexity: Predominantly 2-player games; 3-player extensions (Appendix F.5) are preliminary. No exploration of n-player dynamics or large-scale multi-agent scenarios common in real-world applications

Dataset construction bias: Strategic reasoning ground truth derived from best-performing models (o3, gemini-2.5-pro) may bias evaluation; decision-making evaluation via self-play may not capture robustness against diverse strategies
Limited technical novelty: Benchmark primarily curates and visually adapts existing games (Hanabi, Overcooked, Breakthrough, Pong) rather than introducing fundamentally new multi-agent challenges

Incomplete statistical analysis: Standard deviations missing from Tables 3-4; no significance testing between models; some results show high variability; sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters (temperature, context window) absent
Human experiment design: Only 26 participants with limited details on expertise/training; single evaluation per participant is noisier than repeated measurements
Shallow failure mode analysis: Appendix G provides descriptive examples but lacks systematic categorization, quantitative frequency analysis, or connection to actionable improvements
Underdeveloped persona analysis: Only 3 models tested (Section 4.3, F.3.2); limited investigation of why certain personas work or fail; more systematic analysis needed
